config.title: Balcony Solar in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: What a Balkonkraftwerk makes on a Berlin wall, what it saves, and what the rules ask of a tenant.

items.q: Is there still a subsidy for a Balkonkraftwerk in Berlin?
items.a: No. Berlin used to pay up to 500 euro towards a plug-in solar device through SolarPLUS. The programme reopened on 8 January 2026 with a new structure, SolarPLUS S for homes and SolarPLUS L for larger installations, and a budget of 13 million euro, and the balcony module was not part of it. IBB Business Team, which administers the programme, states that Module E Steckersolargeraete is no longer funded, because the devices are now economic without support. Applications already submitted are still being processed, but new ones are not accepted. Checked on 13 September 2026.

items.q: How much electricity does a balcony solar panel make in Berlin?
items.a: For 800 watt peak of module with a clean view of the sky in central Berlin, modelled on the long-run PVGIS average: 595 kWh a year flat against a south railing, 415 facing east, 403 facing west, and 153 facing north. Laid back at 30 degrees facing south it reaches 810 kWh, which is the best case anywhere in the city. Those are unshaded numbers. A ground-floor balcony with a building across the courtyard will be well below them, and no bracket fixes that.

items.q: Is a Balkonkraftwerk worth it in Berlin now that the grant has gone?
items.a: On most balconies, yes, but the payback comes from a smaller number than people expect. Only the electricity you use at the moment it is made becomes money, because the standard arrangement for these devices gives your surplus to the grid unpaid. A flat drawing about 130 watts in the background keeps 306 of the 595 kWh a south-facing railing kit makes. At 37.93 cents per kilowatt hour, the Vattenfall Berlin basic tariff since 1 April 2026, that is 116 euro a year, so a 400 euro kit pays for itself in roughly three and a half years and then keeps going.

items.q: Should I buy the biggest kit I can, up to 2,000 watt peak?
items.a: Usually not, and this is the most expensive mistake in balcony solar. On the same south railing, going from 800 to 2,000 watt peak of module lifts production from 595 kWh to 1,318 kWh, but a flat drawing 130 watts in the background keeps only 379 kWh instead of 306. The saving moves from 116 euro to 144 euro a year, for several hundred euro of extra panel, and above 960 watt peak you also need a proper feed-in socket fitted by an electrician. If somebody is home during the day and the background draw is nearer 320 watts, the picture reverses: 800 watt peak saves 199 euro and 2,000 watt peak saves 287.

items.q: Flat against the railing or tilted out?
items.a: Flat is fine, and on a Berlin balcony it is usually the better trade. Tilting a south-facing kit to 30 degrees raises production from 595 kWh to 810, but most of that extra arrives at midday in June when the flat is empty and the surplus is given away, so the gain in kilowatt hours you actually keep is about 55, worth roughly 21 euro a year. The vertical panel also beats the tilted one in November, December and January, because it faces the low winter sun head on. It sheds snow and it is not a sail in an autumn storm.

items.q: My balcony faces north. Is it hopeless?
items.a: Not if you change the angle instead of the wall. Flat against a north railing an 800 watt peak kit makes only 153 kWh a year. Laid back at 30 degrees on the same north balcony it makes 458 kWh, and because that output is spread thinly across the day a normal flat keeps 323 of them. That is more kept electricity than a south balcony with the panels bolted flat to the railing. The angle is a bigger lever than the compass.

items.q: Can my landlord say no to a balcony solar panel?
items.a: Not easily any more. Since early October 2024 a plug-in solar device is a privileged measure in the German civil code, so you still ask the landlord or the owners association for consent, but a refusal now needs a concrete reason for your specific case. Not liking how it looks is no longer enough. Ask in writing and keep it short: what you want to hang, where, how it is fastened, and that it is a certified device inside the 800 watt limit.

items.q: Do I need a permit or have to register it in Berlin?
items.a: No building permit. The Senate solar advice service states that under the Bauordnung Berlin no Baugenehmigung is needed for a balcony system on a rented flat. A listed building is the exception and needs the district Denkmalbehoerde, which is a real question in much of Prenzlauer Berg, Mitte and Charlottenburg. You do have to register the device in the Marktstammdatenregister within a month of switching it on, with a handful of fields. Since 16 May 2024 you no longer notify your grid operator separately, and the operator has to fit a two-way meter and swap an old analogue disc at no cost to you.

items.q: Can I just plug it into a normal socket?
items.a: Yes, within limits. The product standard DIN VDE V 0126-95 has been in force since 1 December 2025, and the Verbraucherzentrale Berlin reads it as allowing a certified device to be connected to an ordinary Schuko socket with up to 960 watt peak of module behind the 800 watt inverter. Above that you need a proper feed-in socket installed by an electrician. Only one such device is permitted per household. In a Berlin Altbau on original circuits, one conversation with an electrician before you order is money well spent.

items.q: When is the best time to buy one?
items.a: Any time, but know what you are buying into. A south-facing vertical kit makes about 63 kWh in September and roughly 89 kWh across November, December and January put together, so a panel bought this week will look disappointing for its first three months. That is the shape of the Berlin year, not a fault in the hardware. Hang it, read your own meter through one winter, and judge it in June.
